The statement never assumes V and W finite-dimensional. The cited definitions only define coordinate matrices and change-of-basis matrices for finite ordered bases, so the displayed formula is not well-formed for arbitrary spaces with ordered bases.

Step 2.1 concludes that the chromatic number is 4, but F1 states only the adjacent-vertices condition for proper colourings. It never supplies the definition of chromatic number as the least number of colours, so that inference is uncited.

Step 1.2 asserts that the polygonal cycle has exactly two faces without citing the polygonal Jordan curve theorem; Euler's formula does not license that face count. The same uncited separation is used to count the four faces in step 2.1.

ds: Step 1.1 claims that inserting a spanning tree does not split the containing face, citing [L5] which only states that a plane forest has exactly one face. This does not justify the claim; a lemma about the effect of insertion on face count is missing.
terra: L4 does not faithfully restate its citation: the cited theorem states the vertex-edge-component identity for every forest, not the specialized claim that a tree on n vertices has n-1 edges.

ds: Step 2.1 claims that for a disconnected plane graph, adding noncrossing edges through the unbounded face connects all components. If a component is nested inside a bounded face of another, it does not touch the unbounded face, so the construction fails. The proof does not handle nested components.
terra: Step 3.1 treats L2 as an equality, but L2 only states 3 times the face count is at most 2m. It cites no face-handshake equality, so m=3n-6 is not established.

ds: The fact [L2] states 'If every facial boundary walk has length at least g, then g|F|≤2|E|' but omits the hypothesis that the graph is connected, which the cited lemma requires. This makes [L2] an inaccurate restatement of its dependency.
terra: Step 3.1 is false for a fixed embedding: a component may lie inside a cycle of another component, so it cannot be joined through the unbounded face. The proof must instead use containing faces or first re-embed the components.

The sentence saying edge addition and the underlying abstract graph follow def-graph-deletion-contraction-minor-and-subdivision mis-cites that item: it defines deletions, contractions, minors, and subdivisions, but neither edge addition nor the underlying graph of a plane embedding.

The definition calls G star a finite multigraph, but its cited plane-graph definition does not establish that the face set is finite. Finiteness of faces requires the separate face-finiteness lemma, which is neither cited nor justified here.

The definition does not make the vertex set well-defined: a straight segment admits subdivisions with arbitrary interior breakpoints, so the same polygonal arc has different claimed vertex sets. Later use of a polygon's finite edge and vertex sets therefore has no defined object.
F2 omits the cited definition's length-at-least-three condition. Under F2 the two-edge closed walk u,v,u qualifies, but the cited item says it is not a cycle, so the fact is not a faithful citation.

ds: Step 1.1 cites [L2] to get a minimum proper separation of order at most two. [L2] is the Whitney path characterization and says nothing about separations. The step lacks a valid justification; the cited fact does not license the move.

Step 2.1 claims the two faces lie on opposite sides of C, citing only L2 which gives regions of C. It does not justify why they cannot both lie on the same side while sharing boundary H. This is a logical gap.
terra: Step 1.1 wrongly infers that every non-bridge boundary edge lies on a cycle from L1. L1 states only that cycle edges have two incident faces and bridges one; it does not give the needed converse, so the existence of C is unsupported.

ds: Step 1.1 asserts branch sets are minimal trees, citing only [F1] (minor definition). [F1] does not support this claim. The forward direction from minor to subdivision lacks any valid justification.
terra: Step 1.1 assumes a branch-set model for any minor and minimizes it, but F1 only defines minors by deletion and contraction. No cited fact establishes the equivalence to branch-set models, so the central minor-to-subdivision argument is unsupported.

ds: Step 3.1 is unjustified: it claims a small detour joins the two sides of a bridge without citing any lemma or providing a valid argument. The proof does not establish the required face incidence.
terra: Step 3.1 is not licensed: L2 only identifies a bridge and gives no complement path joining its local sides. The asserted detour through the component complement is neither proved nor cited; the listed polygonal-arc lemma is never invoked, so the one-face conclusion does not follow.

Step 1.1 applies double counting with the face set as an index set, but no cited fact establishes that the face set is finite. The required face-finiteness lemma exists on the page but is not a dependency, so L1's hypotheses are not met.

ds: Step 1.2 cites [L2] to claim an arc not closing a cycle does not split a face, but [L2] only states the arc does not separate the whole plane, not that it does not separate a given face. Likewise, [L1] alone does not imply a polygon splits a face into two. The induction step is unsupported.
terra: Step 1.2 misuses L2: connectedness of the plane minus one arc does not by itself show that adding that arc to an arbitrary existing drawing leaves its containing face connected. The crucial no-splitting assertion is not established.

ds: Step 1.1 constructs arc B via a 'polygonal regular neighbourhood' with no supporting lemma cited, and the reference to the general-position ray lemma is irrelevant. The existence of B is not established, so the proof is incomplete.
terra: Step 2.1 invokes polygonal connectedness of the Jordan regions, but its cited F1 and L1 give only the path definition and the two-region Jordan conclusion. The required open-component corollary is mentioned in the statement but never supplied as a fact or cited in the step.

ds: Step 1.2 claims that rotating a ray changes intersection parity in specific ways (tangential crossing creates/destroys two intersections, passing a vertex changes count by two) with no supporting fact or lemma. [L1] only gives existence of a general-position ray, not these properties. The proof is unjustified.
terra: Step 1.2 wrongly says that a tangency to a polygonal edge creates or destroys two intersections. A straight ray can meet a nonparallel line segment at most once, and for a parallel direction no such two-crossing event occurs. Thus its event analysis does not justify parity invariance.

ds: Fact [L2] misstates the cited theorem by adding 'in particular ℝ', which is not in the source and asserts an unsupported claim that ℝ is a complete ordered field.
terra: Step 2.1 concludes that the union of the per-edge intersection sets is finite, but cites only F1, which merely defines a polygonal path. It never cites the finite-union result or states the needed pairwise disjointness; the mentioned sum rule is not a fact used by the step.

ds: Step 2.1 claims that deleting one edge from a subdivision of K5 or K_{3,3} leaves its branch vertices connected, which is false (e.g., deleting an internal edge of a subdivided path disconnects the two branch vertices). The argument for S empty is therefore unjustified.

terra: The statement never assumes G is finite, but L1 applies only to finite graphs and step 2.1 takes a least cardinality among components. The proof is therefore not licensed for the stated class of graphs.

ds: Step 3.1 claims that if Y is not contained in a single X-arc, then either two Y alternate with two X (yielding K3,3) or x,y have three common neighbors (yielding K5). This overlooks the case where Y consists of exactly two common neighbors separated on C by another X vertex; in that case the condition fails but neither alternating disposition nor three common neighbors hold, yet the graph may be planar and without forbidden minors. The proof gives no argument to exclude this configuration.
terra: Step 1.2 uses transitivity of the minor relation to infer that H excludes both forbidden minors, but its tag cites only L1 and the induction hypothesis. Neither establishes transitivity, so this exclusion is unsupported as written.

ds: Step 2.1 claims S U C divides the side into k regions citing only [L3] (polygonal Jordan curve theorem), but [L3] does not justify that a tree attached to a cycle yields exactly k regions. This gap breaks the proof of the forward implication.

Step 2.1 claims that vertices on the two boundary portions lie in different components of G-v, based on an intuitive geometric argument that a path avoiding v would cross the face boundary. This step is not justified by any cited fact nor by a rigorous topological argument, leaving a logical gap.
terra: Step 3.1's final inference is invalid as cited: a closed walk with no repeated vertex need not be a cycle, since a length-two backtrack has that property. The proof never rules out this case by showing the edge would be a bridge and that two-connectivity forbids it.

ds: Title claims equivalence for all plane graphs of order >=3, but proof assumes two-connectivity. Facts block omits this hypothesis, so the proof is not valid for general plane graphs. Title overstates what is proved.
terra: The title drops the two-connectivity hypothesis. The statement and proof only address two-connected plane graphs, and no step proves that maximality supplies two-connectivity, so the title asserts more than this item establishes.

ds: The forward implication uses [L2] to call the embedding a triangulation, but [L2] restates prop-maximal-plane-triangulation-characterisation without its two-connected hypothesis. The proof does not show the embedding is two-connected, so the step is unjustified.
terra: L2 drops the cited proposition's two-connectedness hypothesis: it applies only to two-connected plane graphs. Step 1.1 never establishes that an embedding of a maximally planar graph is two-connected before using L2.

ds: Step 1.1 claims a leaf exists via the low-degree vertex lemma, but the tags cite [L1] (the edge-count formula) which does not license that move. The required citation is missing, and the cited fact does not support the step.
terra: Step 1.1 misstates the low-degree lemma: it guarantees a vertex of degree at most one, which may be isolated in a forest that also has an edge. No cited fact establishes the required leaf for the deletion step.

ds: Step 1.1 asserts the spanning tree has |V|-1 edges without citing any theorem that states this. [L1] only gives existence of a spanning tree, not its edge count. The step is unjustified.
terra: Step 1.2 claims that adding a cycle-closing edge splits one old face into two. L2 only states face incidence of an edge in an already drawn plane graph; it does not establish the comparison with the preceding drawing or the asserted face-count change.

[L3] omits the cited lemma's essential hypotheses: five distinct cyclic neighbours, coloured 1 through 5, in the graph with v deleted. As written it asserts an unqualified impossibility that the cited item does not state.
L3 drops the finiteness hypothesis: its cited lemma applies only to three-connected finite graphs, but L3 asserts it for every three-connected graph.

ds: Proof forms (G*)* without verifying G* is a plane graph under the simplicity hypothesis; step 2.1 calls drawing a 'plane embedding' but does not ensure the dual definition applies, and steps 3.1–4.1 claim isomorphism without using the condition. Title also asserts double dual identification unconditionally, contrary to the statement.
terra: Steps 3.1 and 4.1 form the dual of G star without assuming G star is simple. For G equal to K2, its dual has a loop, so it is not a plane graph and its dual is undefined under the cited definition.

ds: Step 1.1 claims points near an edge have opposite parity and thus both classes nonempty, but this is not justified by [L1], which only gives local constancy in the complement and does not imply a parity change across the polygon.

terra: Step 1.2 applies induction to G-v without establishing or citing that deleting a vertex from a planar graph preserves planarity. L1 only supplies a low-degree vertex, and the deletion definition does not state this preservation.

[L1] omits the cited proposition's condition that the product be nonzero before asserting its degree bound. Over a ring with zero divisors a nonzero product can be zero, whose degree is undefined, so this restatement is stronger than its source.

ds: Step 1.1 claims that 2c is nonzero because c is nonzero, but this requires that Z has no zero divisors. The only cited fact about Z is [L2] (it is a commutative ring), which does not imply that property. The step is therefore unjustified by its cited facts.
terra: Step 1.1 asserts that 2c is nonzero for every nonzero integer c, but L2 only gives that Z is a commutative ring. It never cites or proves that Z has no zero divisors or the needed cancellation, so the degree argument is not licensed.

L4 is not faithful to its citation: the cited theorem gives evaluation for one polynomial variable, not evaluation determined by images of several indeterminates. Step 3.1 relies on this unsupported bivariate version.
L1 omits the cited criterion's hypotheses: it holds only for a nonzero polynomial over a field and a root in a field extension, not for an arbitrary root as L1 states.
Fact L1 omits the cited theorem's required positive-degree hypothesis, so it states a stronger reduction criterion than its source.

Fact L2 does not faithfully state Eisenstein's criterion: it merely refers to the stated prime-divisibility conditions and omits the required hypotheses, including positive degree, primality, leading coefficient not divisible by p, and p squared not dividing the constant term.

ds: [L3] misstates the definition of irreducible: it says the only divisors are units and associates, but the definition only gives the factorization condition. The proof relies on this stronger claim, so the citation is unfaithful.
terra: Step 1.1 is not licensed by L2-L3: from a common divisor being associate to p it concludes a contradiction with the degree bound, but this needs the uncited fact that a nonzero multiple of p in F[x] has degree at least degree p.

ds: Fact [L4] states 'a field is an integral domain' but cites [[def-field]] which defines a field without stating that it is an integral domain. The fact is stronger than the cited item, so step 1.1 relies on an inaccurate restatement.
terra: Fact L4 is stronger than its cited definition: def-field states field axioms but does not state that every field is an integral domain. Step 1.1 relies on this uncited derived result.

[L1] inaccurately restates Eisenstein's criterion: the cited theorem requires a polynomial of positive degree, but [L1] omits that hypothesis and asserts the criterion for every primitive integer polynomial.

The well-definedness claim that any two monic generators of the same ideal are equal is asserted without support from the cited PID or ideal definitions. The listed justification is circular: its proof invokes this definition to identify the gcd.

In step 2.1, showing the next gcd divides each earlier coefficient requires transitivity of divisibility from its divisibility of c_k and c_k's divisibility of those coefficients. No cited fact establishes divisibility transitivity.

ds: Step 2.1 claims the universal divisibility characterization of [L2] gives cont(fg)=cont(f)cont(g). But [L2] alone does not verify that any common divisor of fg's coefficients divides cont(f)cont(g). That requires further gcd facts not cited, so the step is logically unjustified.
terra: In step 2.1, c(f) and c(g) are never defined. The only introduced content notation is cont(f), so the step concludes an equality with an undefined right-hand side rather than the stated formula.

L1 uses the irreducibility definition in F[x], but its cited definition applies only to an integral domain. The proof never establishes or cites that F[x] is an integral domain, so the reducible-case step 2.1 is not licensed.

Step 1.2 uses the convolution formula for the coefficients of fg, but L1 only describes derivative coefficients and L2 only permits finite-sum manipulations. The polynomial-ring definition supplying convolution is neither cited nor stated as a fact.

Step 1.1 infers termination from strictly decreasing natural degrees, but neither cited fact nor the given assumptions supplies the required well-ordering of the natural numbers. This essential termination step is therefore uncited.

Step 2.1 needs that an integer reduces to zero modulo p exactly when p divides it. L3 only supplies a polynomial homomorphism and L4 only identifies the quotient; neither states the quotient map has kernel pZ. Thus the claimed reduced equation and survival claims are uncited.

Step 3 applies steps 1.1–2.1 to a reducibility factorization in Q[x], whose factors are only known to be nonunits. No cited fact establishes that such factors have positive degree, or that positive-degree polynomials are nonunits, so L5 does not justify the equivalence.

[L1] inaccurately states degree bounds for sums and products of nonzero polynomials without requiring the sum or product itself to be nonzero. The cited proposition makes those conditions explicit, since zero has no degree.

L1 overstates its citation: the cited proposition states the top coefficient formula and a conditional degree inequality, but does not state that every higher coefficient vanishes. That extra assertion is essential to step 2.1.
Step 2.1 invokes L2 for F, but L2 requires F to be an integral domain. The item never establishes or cites that a field is an integral domain; L3 only records inverses and commutativity.

Step 1.2 infers from p dividing d that the residue class of x is a root of f and f-prime, but none of its cited facts states that the gcd d divides f and f-prime. L7 is not cited there and its stated version only gives a Bezout identity.

Fact L6 drops the integral-domain hypothesis of its cited definition. The proof applies irreducibility in F[x] without citing or establishing that F[x] is an integral domain, so the stated dependency does not license that use.

L4 only states that an already-known ring homomorphism preserves the operations, but step 2.1 uses it conversely to conclude that c is a homomorphism. The cited definition supplies that converse, so L4 is an unfaithful restatement and does not license the step as written.

Step 1.1 applies L4 to F without establishing or citing that a field is an integral domain. L4 only applies once its coefficient ring is known to be a domain; this is also needed for cancellation in step 2.1.

ds: L2 misstates the universal property: it omits the required choice of image for x. Step 2.1 cites L2 to ‘reduce coefficients’ but does not specify x->x, so the existence of the reduction homomorphism is not properly justified. This is an incorrect/insufficient citation.
terra: Step 2.1 uses degree additivity for G H and for the reduced product to conclude both reductions retain positive degree, but none of L1-L6 supplies a polynomial degree law. Step 3.1 also calls positive-degree reductions nonunits without citing the units theorem for F[x].

Step 1.1 assumes trichotomy of the real order to make the up/down rule a two-colouring, but cites only Ramsey and the definition of a sequence. def-real-order merely defines the order; its remarks defer trichotomy to another theorem.

ds: Step 1.1 cites [L1] (the theorem statement R(3,3)=6) to justify the claim that at vertex 0 three incident edges share a colour, but [L1] does not provide that combinatorial fact. The step lacks proper citation to the strong pigeonhole principle.
terra: Step 1.1 uses the finite pigeonhole principle to obtain three same-coloured incident edges, but its only tag is L1, which states R(3,3)=6. The given hyperlink does not supply a labelled fact stating pigeonhole, so the cited fact does not license the step.

Step 1.2 is tagged [L1], but [L1] only gives existence of some sufficiently long forcing interval; it does not justify the symmetry normalization or the individual forced colours in that step. The cited support is therefore incorrect.

ds: The tree built in step 1.1 consists of colouring functions, not finite sequences of naturals as required by the definition of tree for [L1] (König's lemma for trees of finite sequences). The application of [L1] is therefore unjustified.

Step 2.1 incorrectly claims the binomial theorem gives R(k,k) ≤ binom(2k-2,k-1). The binomial theorem [L2] does not imply that bound; the required fact is thm-finite-graph-ramsey-binomial-bound, which is not cited, leaving the step unjustified.
terra: Step 2.1 asserts the Ramsey binomial bound without citing or stating the finite graph Ramsey bound; its tag [L2, algebra] only licenses the binomial-theorem estimate.

The claim that every nonempty successor-label set has a least member is not licensed by def-nat-order, which only defines the order and says this least-element property is the later well-ordering principle. The definition neither cites that theorem nor justifies the claim.

ds: The induction step assumes a block progression of length at least 2 to extract a difference t. For m=2 the length is 1, so no t is defined, and the construction of new focused progressions fails. The lemma is not proved for m=2, r>1.
terra: Step 3.1 uses the colour of f and its matching positions in the selected blocks, but the induction hypothesis only gives an integer focus, not that f lies in the first block or coloured interval. No strengthened invariant establishes this, so identical block vectors do not license the claim.

Step 1.1’s tag cites only given and F1, neither of which supplies the cardinality argument needed to conclude that fewer than m red neighbours leaves at least n blue neighbours; the finite sum rule is not cited in the step’s tag.

Step 2.1 uses the union-bound inequality for overlapping bad-colouring sets, but cites only L1, which counts functions. Neither L1 nor a cited fact licenses bounding the overlapping union by the sum of its cardinalities, so the existence conclusion is unsupported.

ds: Step 1.2 selects the lexicographically least k-subset among those whose colours admit an infinite homogeneous set, and cites [L2] for this move. [L2] gives least elements only under the natural order on ℕ, not under lex order on [ℕ]^k. No fact is cited to well-order ℕ^k, so the selection is unjustified.
terra: Step 1.2 invokes natural recursion to define a unique infinite enumeration, but cites only L2. L2 supplies least elements, not the recursion theorem or a proof that this iterative prescription defines a function on all naturals.

Step 1.1 uses a maximum of finitely many descendant-height bounds, including selecting such a bound for each successor, but neither the given facts nor its citations establish finite maxima or finite choice. Its tag [given, construct] does not license this step.
L1 inaccurately restates its source: the cited lemma requires X to be finite, but L1 asserts disjoint cycles commute without that hypothesis.
Step 3.1 invokes normality to infer conjugates are in H, but its tag cites only step 2.1 and L1; neither establishes H normal. The normality conclusion is in step 1.1 and is not cited.

ds: Step 2.1 claims a cycle raised to k is identity iff its length divides k, but no cited fact supports this. A lemma establishing that a cycle's order equals its length is needed and not provided.

Step 1.1 concludes sign of k-cycle = (-1)^{k-1} using that a k-cycle factors into k-1 transpositions and sign is a homomorphism, but the sign of a transposition itself is never established. [L1] does not include that a transposition has sign -1. The proof is incomplete.
terra: L1 says a k-cycle is a product of k-1 transpositions, but the cited transposition theorem's statement only asserts some transposition factorization, not its length. Steps 1.1 and 2.1 rely on this stronger, uncited claim.

ds: [L1] claims sign sends every transposition to -1, but its cited items only state that transpositions generate S_n and sign is a homomorphism. The extra claim is unsupported, so step 3.1 relies on an unjustified fact. This is a defect: the fact restates the sources inaccurately.
terra: L1 attributes to the cited sign theorem that sign sends every transposition to -1, but its statement only says sign is a homomorphism and characterizes surjectivity; the generation theorem says nothing about sign. Step 3.1 relies on this unsupported assertion.

The definition sets inv(sigma)=|Inv(sigma)| but never establishes that Inv(sigma) is finite. The cited cardinality item defines |A| only for finite A; neither inline justification nor justified_by supplies finiteness of this subset of n times n.

ds: The definition of cycle type uses 'orbits of the action generated by sigma' without citing any definition of group action or orbit. The two cited dependencies do not define these concepts, so the definition is not well-formed relative to its declared dependencies.
terra: The definition of c_k invokes the action generated by sigma and its orbits, but neither dependency defines that action or the orbit notion. The cited symmetric-group item defines permutations and cycle notation only, so c_k lacks a stated foundation.

ds: Step 2.1 states a factorization of a transposition into adjacent transpositions without proof or citation; cited facts do not support it. The proof depends on this unsubstantiated identity, so the argument is incomplete.
terra: Step 2.1 asserts the adjacent-transposition factorization but cites only step 1.1 and L1, neither of which establishes that identity. No direct verification of the displayed product is supplied.

In step 2.1, L1 only says a cycle fixes points outside its support; it does not establish that alpha(x) remains in alpha's support. That preservation is needed to conclude beta fixes alpha(x), and no cited fact supplies it.

Step 3.1 concludes that equal values of (-1)^r give equal parity, and that (-1)^r=1 gives even r, but L1 only says transpositions reverse inversion sign. No cited fact licenses these parity inferences.
Step 2.1 concludes that sign is a group homomorphism, but its tag cites only L1. The required homomorphism criterion from def-group-homomorphism is neither stated as a fact nor cited in the step.

Step 1.1 relies on the definition of cycle notation and transpositions to evaluate the displayed product, but its tag cites only the Given and L1. L1 supplies a disjoint-cycle decomposition, not the action of cycle symbols; def-symmetric-group is never stated as a fact.

ds: Step 1.1 claims nq nonzero for nonzero q in Q, so Q is torsion-free. It cites L1 (defines Q as set) and L2 (group powers). But no cited fact gives Q an additive group structure, so the claim that nq is defined and nonzero lacks justification.
terra: Step 1.1 does not establish that the additive rationals are abelian, although this is asserted in the statement. L1 only defines rational equivalence classes, and L2 only defines powers in an already given group; neither supplies rational addition or commutativity.

ds: The subgroup B_t is defined as {(tx,x): x in C_p}, but tx denotes multiplication of two elements of C_p. The group C_p under addition has no such operation; the ring structure of Z/p is not cited or given. Thus the construction is not well-defined in the group setting.
terra: The definition of B_t is not well-formed as stated: C_p is used as an additive cyclic group, but t x multiplies two group elements. L4 identifies its additive quotient only and supplies no field or scalar-multiplication structure.
Step 1.1 contradicts L3: partitions are nondecreasing lists, so 3+1 and 2+1+1 are not partitions as written. They must be 1+3 and 1+1+2.

Step 3.1 cites only step 2.1. That step lists elementary divisors but does not establish that columnwise regrouping yields isomorphic invariant-factor decompositions; the required regrouping result is neither cited nor proved.

ds: Refutation states X has three distinct elements but then claims Sym(X) is finite of order 6, which requires |X|=3. The hypothesis does not imply finiteness, so the counterexample is not established as finite, invalidating the refutation.
terra: Step 1.1 only assumes that X has three distinct elements, which does not imply that X is finite or has exactly three elements. For X=R, Sym(X) is not finite and does not have six elements. It must require that X has cardinality three.

Step 1.1 says L1 writes a group of order p^n with factors of order powers of p, but L1 allows arbitrary prime-power orders. Showing every factor prime is p requires an uncited prime-factorization or divisibility argument.

ds: Step 2.1 is mis-tagged [step 1.1] and offers no fact for the non-cyclicity argument; uses undefined 'exponent' without linking to cyclicity. This step is unjustified.
terra: Step 2.1 is unsupported: step 1.1 only treats the squarefree case and does not establish the displayed group's order, its exponent, or that exponent below the order rules out cyclicity.

ds: Steps 2.1-4.1 lack required fact citations: step 2.1 uses prime divisor existence (L4) and Cauchy (L5) without citing them; step 3.1 uses divisibility and correspondence; step 4.1 uses correspondence and order formula. Tags cite only previous steps, not the justifying facts.

terra: Step 2.1 cites only step 1.1, which proves the opposite implication and does not justify that a finite cyclic group is isomorphic to C of its order or has a one-entry invariant-factor list.

ds: Proof of converse (step 2.1) asserts that a cyclic group has a unique subgroup of each possible order, but no cited fact supports this. L4 does not state uniqueness, so the contradiction is unjustified.
terra: Step 2.1 applies Cauchy's theorem to B and C without establishing that p divides either factor order. That requires an order formula for the internal product or Lagrange for subgroups of the cyclic p-group, neither of which is cited or proved.

Step 1.1 says each G(p_i) is an abelian p_i-group of order p_i^a_i, but L1 only states the internal product decomposition and L2 only counts groups already known to have that order. No cited fact establishes this required property.

ds: Step 2.1 claims the order in the product is the lcm of component orders, citing only step 1.1, missing the required citation of [L4] (thm-order-of-element-in-direct-product). Step 3.1 uses the definition of exponent without citing [L2].
terra: Step 2.1 is cited only to step 1.1, which establishes a cardinality formula. It does not license the asserted element-order formula or the claim that every element order divides n_r; the needed direct-product order result is neither cited there nor developed.

The cited external-product definition explicitly says its operation is not yet established to make a group. This definition nevertheless uses a finite direct product as the target of a group isomorphism without citing the theorem that makes that product a group.

ds: The proof only shows existence of an invariant-factor list from the elementary divisors; it does not prove uniqueness (the 'exactly one way' in the statement). Step 3.1 only verifies the constructed list, not that no other list exists.

Step 1.1 claims |p^i C_{p^e} / p^{i+1} C_{p^e}| is trivial or p depending on i<e, with no cited fact giving the orders of these subgroups in a cyclic group. The cited definitions and general theorems do not entail this computation; a critical lemma is missing.
terra: Step 2.1 is unsupported: step 1.1 only computes each cyclic factor, but no cited fact or argument establishes that p-power images and their quotients commute with the product, nor the resulting product order. Thus the displayed formula does not follow from its tag.

In step 3.1, maximality only bounds the order of b; it does not show that its order divides p^m, so p^m b=0 is unproved. This needs the fact that element orders divide the order of a finite p-group, but no such fact is cited.

Step 3.1 asserts that p divides the quotient order when p does not divide |H|, but cites only step 2.1. Neither that step nor any cited fact supplies the quotient order formula together with prime cancellation, so this induction branch is unlicensed.

Step 3.1 applies the induction hypothesis to H without establishing that H is a finite abelian p-group. L1 only supplies a complementary subgroup; no cited fact shows its order is a power of p or that the cyclic factor has prime-power order.

Step 3.1 invokes both the definition of decomposable and Lagrange to obtain G=B⊕C and the strict order inequalities, but its tag cites only step 2.1, which establishes neither. Step 4.1 likewise invokes internal-product recognition without citing L3.
Step 2.1 invokes recovery from successive p-multiple quotients but cites only step 1.1. That step gives a cyclic decomposition; the recovery assertion is supplied by L4, which step 2.1 never cites.

ds: Step 1.1 claims normality puts [N_i,N_j] inside N_i∩N_j, using commutator notation and a property not provided by the cited facts [given, L1, L2, L3]. No definition of commutator or this containment is included, so the step lacks justification.
Step 3.1 tag cites only step 2.1, but the step relies on L1 (unique order-p subgroup lemma) and L2 (Cauchy) without listing them, so the tag does not license the move.
terra: Step 5 applies the induction hypothesis to G/B without proving or citing that B is normal and that G/B is a finite abelian p-group. The cited quotient, correspondence, and size facts do not supply abelianness or p-group status.

ds: Step 2.1 cites only step 1.1, but its claim that p divides |G/G(p)| and the application of Cauchy require facts L4, L2, L7 which are not cited. The step's justification does not license the move.

terra: Step 2.1 is unjustified: pairwise trivial intersections from 1.1 do not show a component meets the product of all others trivially, and no cited fact establishes that an element of that product has order coprime to p_i. This is the essential injectivity claim.
